# Week 34, 2026

Highlights selected from everything kept between August 14, 2026 and August 21, 2026. Items are selected nightly by an automated pipeline and the summaries are machine generated; follow the links to the original sources. See [About](../../about.md) for how selection works.

<img class="section-banner" src="../../../assets/section-digest.svg" alt="">

## The week in brief

<div class="section-brief">
<p>Two prospective evaluations of clinical artificial intelligence (AI) reached different conclusions about readiness for practice. A large language model decision support system tested in an emergency department produced clinically appropriate outputs in 99 of 100 sampled cases, yet clinician adoption fell from 68% to 30% over four weeks, and the authors state the results do not justify deployment, identifying sustained engagement rather than accuracy as the main barrier <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04601-5">[1]</a>. By contrast, a liver malignancy diagnosis system evaluated as an additional reader in a single-arm trial of 10,333 patients met its primary endpoint and identified 51 previously overlooked lesions, though the authors note that comparative prospective studies are still needed <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04589-y">[2]</a>. Suchi Saria&#x27;s discussion of detecting deterioration signals in electronic health records addresses the same implementation challenge from a builder&#x27;s perspective <a href="https://ai-podcast.nejm.org/e/dr-suchi-saria-on-building-ai-that-changes-care">[13]</a>.</p>
<p>For educators, these mixed results land alongside a systematic review showing that medical students&#x27; attitudes toward and familiarity with AI vary widely across educational settings <a href="https://mededu.jmir.org/2026/1/e89411">[4]</a>, a scoping review examining the validity and scalability of AI-driven clinical competency assessment <a href="https://mededu.jmir.org/2026/1/e92826">[7]</a>, and new evidence on when generative AI supports learning versus replaces it <a href="https://aipodcast.education/when-does-ai-help-learning-and-when-does-it-replace-it">[14]</a>. Governance is also in motion: the United States Department of Health and Human Services is soliciting input on regulation, reimbursement, and research for clinical AI <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03094-3">[6]</a>, researchers published a multistage framework for detecting bias in clinical AI systems <a href="https://ai.jmir.org/2026/1/e102146">[5]</a>, and a pediatrician documented harms to minors from chatbot interactions <a href="https://www.statnews.com/2026/08/19/ai-chatbots-children-grooming-mental-health">[8]</a>, a reminder that safety questions extend beyond the clinic into patients&#x27; homes.</p>
<p class="section-brief-date">Written from the items highlighted below; numbered links go to the sources.</p>
</div>
